doc.title: Glenn Zottola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 7, 2020

title: Embellishing the melody like Louis and Bird, not patterns
summary: His father's advice to embellish like Louis, Parker as advanced embellishment, and criticism of pattern-playing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Are there a couple of things that you can relate to people that define a good and memorable melody?
In a song that perhaps could then be transferred to an improvisation.

Well when I was a kid I asked my dad how do you play jazz. And my dad was a great trumpet player, played lead trumpet like Conrad Gozzo and jazz like Louis, and he was a conductor of classical music. He said, “Just embellish the melody like Louis.” And I did that. And that was [inaudible] melody like Louis. And really I wrote in the liner notes to my Charlie Parker with Strings album, I carried that philosophy of embellishing the melody even when it got more advanced like Charlie Parker, ‘cause what Charlie Parker is doing is really similar to what Louis was doing just more advanced. Charlie Parker was still embellishing the melody. So I use the melody as like a guidepost to make these embellishments but it’s always off the melody. It’s not like they teach you in music school, patterns. That’s B.S. You can’t play that way and really, at a high level. Sonny Rollins said you can’t think and play at the same time. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
Now I know what he means by that. You can, but you hear these guys playing and I can hear them thinking okay we’re going to do this pattern, that pattern, this pattern.
It’s like they’re playing what their — they came from the practice room and they’re playing it on a gig I guess.
Yeah. Yeah. That’s not the way Bird played. That’s not the way Coleman Hawkins played. Even though those guys know music.
